title: Triangle detection in CONGEST
formal: For arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex networks, determine the optimal worst-case randomized round complexity of triangle detection in CONGEST, up to constant factors. Each vertex initially knows its distinct \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifier and its neighbors, and may send a separate \(O(\log  n)\)-bit message in each direction of every incident edge per synchronous round. On a triangle-free graph all vertices must output NO; otherwise at least one must output YES. The joint answer must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and identifier assignment. The algorithm is uniform, has private random bits, and may know n. The currently established bounds are $\Omega(\log\log n)$ and $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$.
why: I include this because it isolates the cost of learning one local pattern under network bandwidth constraints. A sharp answer would distinguish the communication needed for deciding existence from the communication needed for distributing all witnesses, and would test how far current lower-bound methods reach.
definitions: $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. Local computation is unrestricted, vertex identifiers have $O(\log n)$ bits, and the communication graph is exactly $G$, not an all-to-all overlay. Nodes may know $n$. The output convention avoids charging the graph diameter merely to inform every vertex of a remote triangle. The triangle is a subgraph on three distinct mutually adjacent vertices.

progress.text: Chang, Pettie, Saranurak, and Zhang give $\widetilde O(n^{1/3})$-round algorithms for triangle enumeration, counting, and detection. The matching enumeration lower bound does not establish the same detection lower bound.
Assadi and Sundaresan prove an $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound for deterministic and randomized detection, providing the first lower bound beyond a single round.
Censor-Hillel’s ADGA survey explicitly retains the round complexity of CONGEST triangle detection as an open problem after incorporating that lower bound.

status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The 2025 multi-round lower bound is included; the detection/listing distinction is essential.

context_blocks.text: Every vertex knows two of the three edges of a triangle containing it. The missing information is whether two of its neighbors are adjacent. If messages had unlimited length, neighbors could exchange their complete adjacency lists in one round. The difficulty comes from fitting the relevant information through bounded-capacity edges.

For example, a vertex with many neighbors cannot simply send its entire neighborhood to every neighbor in one short message. On the other hand, most pairs of its neighbors may be irrelevant, so transmitting every adjacency list can be wasteful. An algorithm must exploit the topology to decide which information needs to move and where it can be combined.

Detection asks for one bit of global evidence, whereas listing requires the network collectively to output every triangle. A graph can contain a cubic number of triangles. Consequently, a lower bound driven by the volume of listed output does not automatically apply to detection. The near-optimal listing algorithm supplies a detection upper bound, but leaves this distinction unresolved.

The 2025 lower bound rules out every fixed number of rounds, including randomized protocols. It changes the old question of whether even two rounds are necessary into a quantitative gap. Conventional two-party communication reductions encounter barriers here, making stronger lower bounds a problem about proof techniques as well as about graph algorithms.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.

importance.reason: Triangle detection is a basic distributed subgraph task. Its exact round complexity calibrates techniques used for many larger patterns.

sentences: Triangle detection asks a distributed network to report whether any three vertices are pairwise adjacent.
In CONGEST, each edge transmits only \(O(\log  n)\) bits per round, even though vertices initially know all their own neighbors.
The saved card asks for the optimal randomized round complexity between the stated doubly logarithmic lower bound and roughly \(n^{1/3}\) upper bound.
Detection needs only one positive witness somewhere in the network, unlike listing every triangle.
The challenge is to exploit that smaller output requirement while still communicating enough information to discover an edge between two neighbors.
